rationale: The entry's core — that sapphire figures the full moon in its enthroned and bridal office, a throne-glory that is reflected rather than possessed — is carried by a tight, checkable chain in the supplied texts: tohar (H2892) genuinely occurs both in Exodus 24:10 ('the body of heaven in his clearness') and in Psalm 89:44 ('thou hast made his glory to cease'), and Psalm 89:36-37 explicitly establishes the same throne 'as the sun' and 'as the moon... a faithful witness in heaven,' a glory that verse 44 says can be made to cease — i.e., worn, not owned. The sapphire throne-likeness of Ezekiel 1:26 and 10:1 sits in the firmament exactly where Psalm 89:37 stations the lunar witness, and the bridal frame is textual, not imposed: Isaiah 54:5 (thy Maker is thine husband) precedes 54:11 (foundations with sapphires); Revelation 21:9 names the bride before 21:19 sets sapphire in her foundations; Song 5:14 places sapphires on the Beloved beside 6:10's 'fair as the moon.' The strongest counter (sapphire = heaven and God's own throne-glory, per the blue/sky association) explains Exodus 24:10 and Ezekiel 1:26 generically but leaves the tohar link to Psalm 89:44, the sun/moon simile of Psalm 89:36-37 printed with the entry, the husband-sapphire pairing in Isaiah 54, and the moon language surrounding sapphire in the Song unaccounted for, and it identifies no supplied text the book's core cannot explain without contradiction. However, the printed assertion 'Identified with Issachar' receives no support anywhere in the supplied evidence — the chapter never mentions Issachar and stone-to-tribe mappings are notoriously unstable — so the scope is CORE_ONLY.
book_core_identification: Sapphire symbolizes the full moon in its enthroned and bridal form: the sapphire likeness marking the place of God's throne, whose brightness (tohar) is a reflected, wearable glory — received from its Head and capable of being made to cease — rather than an owned light.
book_secondary_elaborations: The 'clearness' of Exodus 24:10 is the rare Hebrew word tohar, the same word rendered 'glory' in Psalm 89:44 where the throne-glory is made to cease.
The sapphire brightness is 'worn, not owned' — a reflector's glory that can be removed.
Sapphire is identified with the tribe of Issachar.
Cross-references to the Issachar entry and to The Pearls of Wisdom, ch. 31.
unsupported_glossary_assertions: 'Identified with Issachar' — no supplied scripture, prior finding, or chapter evidence connects sapphire to Issachar; Exodus 28:18 lists the stones without tribal assignments, the supporting chapter never mentions Issachar, and stone-to-tribe mappings vary widely across traditions.
chapter_only_objections: The kisse/keseh (throne/full moon) identification rests on unpointed consonantal wordplay (כסא in Ezekiel 1:26 read as keseh per Proverbs 7:20), which is suggestive but not demonstrative.
The pearl-equals-full-moon chain through Proverbs 3 and 31, including the peninim-as-pearl lexical claim against the traditional 'rubies,' is a chapter-level argument not asserted in the entry.
Several MEAT retranslations (e.g., 'holds fast the circuit' for the distaff, 'laugheth at the last day,' 'whiteness' for snow/scarlet) select alternate lexical senses to fit the lunar portrait.
The Psalm 81 keseh feast-day and calendar-reckoning arguments, and the east-gate/full-moon entrance reading of Ezekiel 46, are chapter applications outside the glossary claim.
The chapter does not address why a blue stone (sapphire/lapis) rather than a white one should picture the white full moon, relying instead on the clearness/brightness vocabulary.
strongest_counter_interpretation: Sapphire symbolizes heaven itself and the throne and glory of God — its sky-blue clarity pointing directly to the divine presence and the celestial realm (Exodus 24:10; Ezekiel 1:26; 10:1; Revelation 21:19), with the bridal and foundation texts (Isaiah 54:11; Revelation 21:19) read simply as the preciousness and restored glory God bestows on His people.
counter_core_identification: Sapphire is a direct symbol of the heavenly realm and God's own throne-glory and transcendent presence, grounded in the theophany texts where sapphire appears beneath God's feet and as the appearance of His throne.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that the sapphire throne-likeness is lunar or bridal at all: on its reading the stone signifies God's own inherent, transcendent glory and the heaven where He dwells, not a subordinate reflector — a created light 'wearing' a glory that can cease. Both identifications cannot be true of the same referent: an inherent divine glory cannot also be a borrowed brightness made to cease per Psalm 89:44.
counter_case: Exodus 24:10 compares the sapphire pavement to 'the body of heaven,' making the sky itself the explicit point of comparison.
Ezekiel 1:26 and 10:1 place the sapphire throne-likeness with the divine occupant above it — most naturally God's own throne, not a lunar emblem.
Revelation 21:19's sapphire foundation sits in a catalog of twelve stones whose collective point is the city's God-given splendor, not a phase of the moon.
The blue color of sapphire/lapis lazuli matches the sky and heaven far more naturally than the white full moon.
This reading is the broad, stable consensus across patristic, medieval, and modern interpretation.
book_explanatory_advantages: The tohar link is a hard lexical fact: the word occurs only four times, joining the sapphire pavement's 'clearness' (Exodus 24:10) to the throne-'glory' that ceases (Psalm 89:44) — a glory that can be removed is worn, not owned, which the counter's 'inherent divine glory' reading cannot say of God.

Psalm 89:36-37, printed with the entry, explicitly renders the throne 'as the sun' and 'as the moon... a faithful witness in heaven,' natively pairing throne-imagery with the lunar witness in the very psalm the tohar link lands in.

The bridal contexts are structural in the cited texts: Isaiah 54:5 (Maker as husband) immediately precedes the sapphire foundations of 54:11; Revelation 21:9 names the bride before the sapphire foundation of 21:19; Song 5:14's sapphires on the Beloved stand two verses from 6:10's 'fair as the moon, clear as the sun.'
Job 37:18, 21 (the sky as a molten mirror whose bright light appears when cleansed) supplies a mechanism for reflected brightness in the same firmament, cohering with the 'brightness worn' claim.
Lamentations 4:7-8 shows sapphire-polish as a splendor that can be lost under judgment — again a worn, removable brightness — which the counter treats as incidental.
counter_explanatory_advantages: It is the simpler and consensus reading, requiring no lexical chains or wordplay.
It directly honors the explicit sky comparison in Exodus 24:10 and sapphire's blue color.
It handles Ezekiel's throne visions with no intermediate lunar step: God sits above a sapphire throne, so sapphire signals divine transcendence.
decisive_sources: Exodus 24:10 with Psalm 89:44 (the shared rare word tohar: clearness/glory that can be made to cease)
Psalm 89:36-37 (the throne established 'as the sun' and 'as the moon,' the faithful witness in heaven)
Ezekiel 1:26 and 10:1 (the sapphire throne-likeness in/above the firmament, the lunar witness's station)
Isaiah 54:5, 11 (Maker as husband; foundations of sapphires)
Revelation 21:9, 19 (the bride, the Lamb's wife; sapphire as her second foundation)
Song of Solomon 5:14 with 6:9-10 (sapphires on the Beloved beside 'fair as the moon')
unresolved_objections: The Issachar identification remains unevidenced in the supplied materials and depends on an external cross-referenced entry not provided.

Sapphire's blue color fits the sky more naturally than the white moon; the book answers via brightness/clarity vocabulary rather than color, which is plausible from the texts but not addressed head-on.
The kisse/keseh consonantal identity, though used only as chapter support, does some quiet work behind the entry's throne-moon pairing and is wordplay rather than explicit statement.
